knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility invariance and linear contraction of the minimax gradient-mapping iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The result combines invariance of the feasible set with squared-distance contraction for every constant stepsize satisfying 0<h≤1/L.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f\in\mathcal{S}^{1,1}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^n) with \mu>0 and L>0, and let x^* be the unique minimizer of f on its feasible set Q. Suppose x_0\in Q and x_{k+1}=x_k-h\,g_f(x_k;L) for k\ge 0. If 0<h\le L^{-1}, then, for every k\ge 0, x_k\in Q and \|x_k-x^*\|^2\le(1-\mu h)^k\|x_0-x^*\|^2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated smooth strongly convex minimax model, the constant-step gradient-mapping iteration remains in the feasible set and contracts squared distance to the unique minimizer by the factor 1−μh per iteration whenever the stepsize is positive and at most 1/L.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is the unique minimizer of }f\text{ on }Q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Windowed best-iterate gradient norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stationarity-progress measure for a differentiable objective and an arbitrary iterate sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a differentiable function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, an iterate sequence $(x_i)_{i\ge0}$, and integers $0\le k\le T$, define $g_{k,T}:=\min_{k\le i\le T}\|\nabla f(x_i)\|$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The best-iterate gradient norm over iterations k through T is the minimum gradient norm attained in that inclusive window.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iterative architecture of smooth unconstrained algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General architecture, including the controlled-nonmonotonicity exception.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a starting point \(x_0\), a smooth unconstrained minimization algorithm generates iterates \(x_{k+1}\) using information about \(f\) at \(x_k\) and possibly at earlier iterates, and terminates when further progress is unavailable or a solution has been approximated to the required accuracy. Monotone schemes seek \(f(x_{k+1})<f(x_k)\); a controlled nonmonotone scheme may omit one-step decrease but prescribes an integer \(m\ge 1\) for which \(f(x_k)<f(x_{k-m})\) at the applicable indices \(k\ge m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth unconstrained optimization algorithm starts from a user- or algorithm-selected point, generates each new iterate using current and possibly past objective information, and stops for lack of progress or sufficient accuracy. Monotone schemes lower the objective at each accepted step; controlled nonmonotone schemes may allow individual increases but require decrease relative to a prescribed earlier iterate.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is a smooth unconstrained objective}
m\in\mathbb{N},\ m\ge 1\quad\text{when a controlled nonmonotone rule is used}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{k+1}\text{ is generated from current and possibly historical information, with either }f(x_{k+1})<f(x_k)\text{ or the prescribed nonmonotone condition }f(x_k)<f(x_{k-m}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity as the Smooth Unconstrained Algorithmic Target
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A guiding principle for algorithms applied to differentiable unconstrained objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a differentiable unconstrained objective $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, the algorithms under consideration seek a stationary point $x^*$ satisfying $\nabla f(x^*)=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth unconstrained optimization algorithms seek points where the objective gradient vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The algorithmic target is an }x^*\text{ such that }\nabla f(x^*)=0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convexity-free stationarity guarantee for a smooth, bounded-below gradient iteration satisfying the stated decrease inequality, including summability, asymptotic stationarity, and a best-iterate rate.

abla f(x_k)$ with $h_k\in\mathbb R$, and suppose that some $\omega>0$ satisfies $f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\ge(\omega/L)\|
abla f(x_k)\|^2$ for every $k\ge0$. If $f^*$ is any lower bound of $f$, then for every $N\ge0$, $(\omega/L)\sum_{k=0}^N\|
abla f(x_k)\|^2\le f(x_0)-f(x_{N+1})\le f(x_0)-f^*$. Hence $
abla f(x_k)	o0$, and, with $g_N^*=\min_{0\le k\le N}\|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Preselected gradient step sizes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A step-selection policy for Euclidean gradient descent; the displayed schedules are examples, not an exhaustive characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the iteration $x_{k+1}=x_k-h_k\nabla f(x_k)$ with $h_k>0$, a preselected step-size policy fixes the entire sequence $\{h_k\}_{k\ge0}$ in advance. Typical choices include $$h_k=h\quad(h>0)$$ and $$h_k=\frac{h}{\sqrt{k+1}}\quad(h>0).$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A preselected step-size policy fixes all positive gradient-descent step sizes before the iterations start. Typical examples are a positive constant step and a step proportional to one over the square root of the iteration index plus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{h_k\}_{k\ge0}\text{ is fixed in advance; typical choices are }h_k=h\text{ or }h_k=h/\sqrt{k+1}\text{ with }h>0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity of Limit Points under Gradient-Related Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit-point stationarity for gradient iterations using the minimization, limited-minimization, or Armijo rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha^k d^k, and suppose that \{d^k\} is gradient related to \{x^k\}. If \alpha^k is chosen by the minimization rule, the limited minimization rule, or the Armijo rule, then every limit point \bar x of \{x^k\} is stationary for f.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a gradient iteration with gradient-related directions, use of the minimization, limited-minimization, or Armijo rule ensures that every limit point of the iterates is stationary.
assumptions_latex: \alpha^k\text{ is chosen by the minimization, limited-minimization, or Armijo rule}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ a limit point of }\{x^k\}\Longrightarrow\nabla f(\bar x)=0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constant-step scheme II for a max-type minimization problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here q_f is the condition ratio from the surrounding max-type problem model, and x_f(y;L) is its prescribed model update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and
\[
\alpha_0\in\left[\sqrt{q_f},\frac{2(3+q_f)}{3+\sqrt{21+4q_f}}\right],\qquad y_0=x_0.
\]
For \(k=0,1,2,\ldots\), evaluate \(\{f_i(y_k),\nabla f_i(y_k)\}_{i=1}^m\), set
\[
x_{k+1}=x_f(y_k;L),
\]
choose \(\alpha_{k+1}\in(0,1)\) satisfying
\[
\alpha_{k+1}^2=(1-\alpha_{k+1})\alpha_k^2+q_f\alpha_{k+1},
\]
and set
\[
\beta_k=\frac{\alpha_k(1-\alpha_k)}{\alpha_k^2+\alpha_{k+1}},\qquad y_{k+1}=x_{k+1}+\beta_k(x_{k+1}-x_k).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, evaluate every smooth component and its gradient at the extrapolated point, perform the prescribed max-type model update, update the acceleration parameter through its scalar equation, and extrapolate using the resulting momentum coefficient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularization-parameter comparison for gradient models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An abstract comparison principle requiring only the stated model inequality; no ordering between the two positive parameters is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that for every \gamma>0 and \bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n there are x_f(\bar x;\gamma)\in Q, g_f(\bar x;\gamma)\in\mathbb{R}^n, and f^*(\bar x;\gamma)\in\mathbb{R} such that, for every x\in Q, f(\bar x;x)+\frac{\gamma}{2}\|x-\bar x\|^2\ge f^*(\bar x;\gamma)+\langle g_f(\bar x;\gamma),x-\bar x\rangle+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\|g_f(\bar x;\gamma)\|^2. Then, for all \gamma_1,\gamma_2>0 and \bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n, f^*(\bar x;\gamma_2)\ge f^*(\bar x;\gamma_1)+\frac{\gamma_2-\gamma_1}{2\gamma_1\gamma_2}\|g_f(\bar x;\gamma_1)\|^2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any gradient-model quantities satisfying the stated quadratic lower inequality obey a comparison formula across every pair of positive regularization parameters. The formula remains valid when the second parameter is smaller, in which case its correction term is negative.
assumptions_latex: \forall\gamma>0,\ \forall\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ x_f(\bar x;\gamma)\in Q,\ g_f(\bar x;\gamma)\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ f^*(\bar x;\gamma)\in\mathbb{R}
\forall x\in Q:\ f(\bar x;x)+\frac{\gamma}{2}\|x-\bar x\|^2\ge f^*(\bar x;\gamma)+\langle g_f(\bar x;\gamma),x-\bar x\rangle+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\|g_f(\bar x;\gamma)\|^2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical quadratic form of the estimate functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The scalar recurrence is read consistently with the stated sequence of minimum values, so its leading term is \((1-\alpha_k)\phi_k^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(k\ge0\),
\[
\phi_k(x)\equiv\phi_k^*+\frac{\gamma_k}{2}\|x-v_k\|^2,
\]
where \(v_0=x_0\), \(\phi_0^*=f(x_0)\), and
\[
\gamma_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)\gamma_k+\alpha_k\mu,
\]
\[
v_{k+1}=\frac{(1-\alpha_k)\gamma_kv_k+\alpha_k\mu y_k-\alpha_kg_f(y_k;L)}{\gamma_{k+1}},
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi_{k+1}^*={}&(1-\alpha_k)\phi_k^*+\alpha_k\left(f(x_f(y_k;L))+\frac{1}{2L}\|g_f(y_k;L)\|^2\right)\\
&+\frac{\alpha_k^2}{2\gamma_{k+1}}\|g_f(y_k;L)\|^2
+\frac{\alpha_k(1-\alpha_k)\gamma_k}{\gamma_{k+1}}
\left(\frac{\mu}{2}\|y_k-v_k\|^2+\langle g_f(y_k;L),v_k-y_k\rangle\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every estimate function remains a quadratic with curvature γ_k, center v_k, and minimum value φ_k^*. These three quantities obey the displayed explicit recurrences.
assumptions_latex: \phi_k\text{ is the recursively defined estimate-function sequence}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-momentum method for a smooth-component max-type problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here q_f=mu/L is supplied by the stated smooth strongly convex problem class, and x_f(y;L) denotes the prescribed max-type update. The extract itself gives no convergence claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f\in\mathcal{S}^{1,1}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^n)\), choose \(x_0\in Q\), set \(y_0=x_0\), and define
\[
\beta=\frac{1-\sqrt{q_f}}{1+\sqrt{q_f}}.
\]
For \(k=0,1,2,\ldots\), evaluate \(\{f_i(y_k),\nabla f_i(y_k)\}_{i=1}^m\), set
\[
x_{k+1}=x_f(y_k;L),
\]
and then set
\[
y_{k+1}=x_{k+1}+\beta(x_{k+1}-x_k).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize at x_0, select the constant momentum coefficient from the condition ratio, and repeatedly evaluate all smooth components, perform the prescribed max-type update, and extrapolate using the difference of the two most recent iterates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual certificate for approximate constrained optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of the scheme's model residual into objective-target and constraint tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $t_k\in\mathbb R$, $x_{k,j}\in\mathbb R^n$, $L>0$, and $\epsilon\ge0$. If $f^*(t_k;x_{k,j};L)\le\epsilon$ and $x_*:=x_f(t_k;x_{k,j};L)$, then $f(t_k;x_*)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\{f_0(x_*)-t_k,\,f_i(x_*)\}\le\epsilon$. If additionally $t_k\le t^*$, then $f_0(x_*)\le t^*+\epsilon$ and $f_i(x_*)\le\epsilon$ for every $i=1,\ldots,m$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model residual no larger than epsilon certifies that the generated point's objective-target residual and every constraint residual are at most epsilon. If the current target is no larger than the optimal value, the point is epsilon-feasible and its objective is at most the optimum plus epsilon.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Constraints as an Indicator Composite
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The set is convex, but convexity of the smooth objective is not asserted by the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{E}\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(C\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}(f))\), and let \(f\) be \(L_f\)-smooth on \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}(f))\). If \(g=\delta_C\), then \[\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{E}}\{f(\mathbf{x})+\delta_C(\mathbf{x})\}=\min_{\mathbf{x}\in C}f(\mathbf{x}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex set C contained in the interior of dom(f), adding its indicator function to an L_f-smooth objective is equivalent to minimizing that objective over C.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne C\subseteq\mathbb{E},\quad C\text{ is closed and convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Master process with an internal minimization scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic specification of the two-level constrained minimization scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $Q$, $\kappa\in(0,\tfrac12)$, $t_0<t^*$, $\epsilon>0$, and $x_0\in Q$, for each master iteration $k\ge0$ run method $(2.3.13)$ on $f(t_k;\cdot)$ from $x_{k,0}=x_k$ until the first $j(k)$ satisfying $f^*(t_k;x_{k,j(k)};\mu)\ge(1-\kappa)f^*(t_k;x_{k,j(k)};L)$. Choose $j^*(k)\in\arg\min_{0\le j\le j(k)}f^*(t_k;x_{k,j};L)$, set $x_{k+1}=x_f(t_k;x_{k,j^*(k)};L)$, and update $t_{k+1}=t^*(x_{k,j(k)},t_k)$. Stop globally if some generated internal iterate satisfies $f^*(t_k;x_{k,j};L)\le\epsilon$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each outer iteration, approximately minimize the current parameterized model until the prescribed comparison between the mu- and L-based residuals holds. Use the best encountered L-residual to form the next primal point, update the master parameter from the terminal internal iterate, and stop when any internal L-residual is at most epsilon.
assumptions_latex: Q\text{ is the prescribed set},\quad x_0\in Q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parametric max-model value and root
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a quadratically regularized max-type model over Q and the root associated with its minimum value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \bar{x}\in Q,\ t\in\mathbb{R}, and \mu>0, define
\[
f_\mu(t;\bar{x};x)=\max\!\left\{f_0(\bar{x})+\langle\nabla f_0(\bar{x}),x-\bar{x}\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-\bar{x}\|^2-t,\ \max_{1\le i\le m}\left[f_i(\bar{x})+\langle\nabla f_i(\bar{x}),x-\bar{x}\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-\bar{x}\|^2\right]\right\},
\]
and
\[
f^*(t;\bar{x};\mu)=\min_{x\in Q}f_\mu(t;\bar{x};x).
\]
The notation t^*(\bar{x},t) denotes a root of the scalar function s\mapsto f^*(s;\bar{x};\mu).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a reference point, form the maximum of the quadratically regularized affine objective model shifted by the scalar parameter and the corresponding constraint models. Minimize this maximum over Q; the stated t-star notation denotes a root of the resulting scalar value function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower bound for the next estimate-sequence minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A conditional estimate-sequence recursion in the notation and setting inherited from the referenced preceding lemma.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume the setting and notation of Lemma 2.20 and suppose \(\phi_k^*\ge f(x_k)\). Then
\[
f(x_k)\ge f(x_f(y_k;L))+\langle g_f(y_k;L),x_k-y_k\rangle+\frac{1}{2L}\|g_f(y_k;L)\|^2+\frac{\mu}{2}\|x_k-y_k\|^2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi_{k+1}^*\ge{}&(1-\alpha_k)f(x_k)+\alpha_k f(x_f(y_k;L))
+\left(\frac{\alpha_k}{2L}-\frac{\alpha_k^2}{2\gamma_{k+1}}\right)\|g_f(y_k;L)\|^2\\
&+\frac{\alpha_k(1-\alpha_k)\gamma_k}{\gamma_{k+1}}\langle g_f(y_k;L),v_k-y_k\rangle\\
\ge{}&f(x_f(y_k;L))+\left(\frac{1}{2L}-\frac{\alpha_k^2}{2\gamma_{k+1}}\right)\|g_f(y_k;L)\|^2\\
&+(1-\alpha_k)\left\langle g_f(y_k;L),\frac{\alpha_k\gamma_k}{\gamma_{k+1}}(v_k-y_k)+x_k-y_k\right\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the preceding lemma's setting, if the current estimate-sequence minimum dominates f(xₖ), the stated first-order lower model at yₖ bounds f(xₖ). Substitution into the estimate-sequence recursion gives the displayed two-stage lower bound on the next minimum φ*ₖ₊₁.
assumptions_latex: \text{The setting and notation of Lemma 2.20 hold}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient Mapping and Reduced Gradient of a Regularized Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The minimizing point is called the gradient mapping in the extract; the associated scaled displacement is the reduced gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty, let $\gamma>0$, and let $f_\gamma:\mathbb{R}^n\times Q\to\mathbb{R}$. For each $\bar{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$, define $f^*(\bar{x};\gamma)=\min_{x\in Q}f_\gamma(\bar{x};x)$ and $X_f(\bar{x};\gamma)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}f_\gamma(\bar{x};x)$. If $X_f(\bar{x};\gamma)\ne\varnothing$, any selection $x_f(\bar{x};\gamma)\in X_f(\bar{x};\gamma)$ is a gradient mapping, and its reduced gradient is $g_f(\bar{x};\gamma)=\gamma(\bar{x}-x_f(\bar{x};\gamma))$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a parameterized model minimized over a nonempty set, any attained minimizing point is termed a gradient mapping, and gamma times its displacement from the base point is the corresponding reduced gradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Telescoping bound on cumulative internal iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An abstract cumulative-work estimate obtained by summing stagewise logarithmic bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\in\mathbb N\), and let \(j(0),\ldots,j(N)\in\mathbb R\) be nonnegative. Assume that \(Q_f>0\), \(L>\mu>0\), \(\kappa>0\), and \(\Delta_0,\ldots,\Delta_{N+1}>0\), and that for every \(k\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\), \[j(k)\le 1+\sqrt{Q_f}\ln\frac{2(L-\mu)}{\kappa\mu}+\sqrt{Q_f}\ln\frac{\Delta_k}{\Delta_{k+1}}.\] Then \[\sum_{k=0}^{N}j(k)\le (N+1)\left[1+\sqrt{Q_f}\ln\frac{2(L-\mu)}{\kappa\mu}\right]+\sqrt{Q_f}\ln\frac{\Delta_0}{\Delta_{N+1}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every nonnegative stage count satisfies the stated constant-plus-log-ratio estimate, summing those estimates telescopes the consecutive Delta ratios and gives the displayed cumulative bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear convergence of fixed-momentum accelerated gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global objective-gap rate for the exact gradient iteration with stepsize 1/L.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, \(\mu\)-strongly convex, and have \(L\)-Lipschitz continuous gradient, where \(0<\mu\le L\). Let \(x^*\in\arg\min f\), set \(f^*=f(x^*)\), initialize \(x_{-1}=x_0\), and put
\[
\beta=\frac{1-\sqrt{\mu/L}}{1+\sqrt{\mu/L}}.
\]
For \(k\ge0\), define
\[
y_k=x_k+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1}),\qquad x_{k+1}=y_k-\frac1L\nabla f(y_k).
\]
Then, for every integer \(k\ge0\),
\[
f(x_k)-f^*\le2\left(1-\sqrt{\frac\mu L}\right)^k\bigl(f(x_0)-f^*\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an L-smooth, μ-strongly convex differentiable objective, accelerated gradient with stepsize 1/L, the stated fixed momentum, and x_{-1}=x_0 has objective gap at most twice (1−sqrt(μ/L))^k times the initial gap.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence bounds for the variable-momentum max-type scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The initialization formula is well-defined only when alpha_0<1; with the stated interval this excludes q_f=1. The exponential fraction is directly defined for mu>0. At mu=0 it has a removable 0/0 singularity, and its continuous extension is the displayed polynomial bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\mathcal{S}^{1,1}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^n)\) be max-type, let \(X^*\ne\varnothing\), set \(f^*=\inf_x f(x)\), choose \(x^*\in X^*\), and put \(q_f=\mu/L\) with \(0\le q_f<1\). Suppose
\[
\alpha_{k+1}^2=(1-\alpha_{k+1})\alpha_k^2+q_f\alpha_{k+1},\qquad
\beta_k=\frac{\alpha_k(1-\alpha_k)}{\alpha_k^2+\alpha_{k+1}},
\]
\[
x_{k+1}=x_f(y_k;L),\qquad y_{k+1}=x_{k+1}+\beta_k(x_{k+1}-x_k),
\]
and
\[
\alpha_0\in\left[\sqrt{q_f},\frac{2(3+q_f)}{3+\sqrt{21+4q_f}}\right],\qquad
\gamma_0=\frac{\alpha_0(\alpha_0L-\mu)}{1-\alpha_0}>\mu.
\]
Then, for every \(k\ge0\),
\[
f(x_k)-f^*\le
\frac{4L}{(\gamma_0-\mu)(k+1)^2}
\left[f(x_0)-f^*+\frac{\gamma_0}{2}\|x_0-x^*\|^2\right].
\]
If \(\mu>0\), then also
\[
f(x_k)-f^*\le
\frac{4\mu\left[f(x_0)-f^*+\frac{\gamma_0}{2}\|x_0-x^*\|^2\right]}
{(\gamma_0-\mu)\left[\exp\!\left(\frac{k+1}{2}\sqrt{q_f}\right)-\exp\!\left(-\frac{k+1}{2}\sqrt{q_f}\right)\right]^2}.
\]
For \(\mu=0\), the continuous extension of the latter expression equals the polynomial bound above.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated well-defined initialization, the variable-momentum exact max-type update has an O(1/(k+1)^2) objective-gap bound. When μ is positive it also has the displayed condition-sensitive exponential bound; at μ=0 that expression must be understood through its continuous extension. The endpoint q_f=1 is not covered by the displayed initialization formula.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-max minimization with smooth components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a finite-max objective built from smooth components and its minimization over a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be closed and convex, and let f_i\in\mathcal{S}_{\mu,L}^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^n,\|\cdot\|) for i=1,\ldots,m. Define
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x).
\]
The smooth minimax problem is
\[
\min_{x\in Q}f(x)=\min_{x\in Q}\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x).
\]
The function f is a max-type function composed of the f_i; the notation f\in\mathcal{S}_{\mu,L}^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^n,\|\cdot\|) means that every component f_i belongs to that class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given finitely many components in the same smooth convexity class, their pointwise maximum is a max-type function. The associated problem minimizes that maximum over a closed convex set; the components are smooth, although their maximum need not be differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x),\qquad \min_{x\in Q}f(x)=\min_{x\in Q}\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Outer-start objective-gap bound and its nonnegativity requirement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extracted assumptions bound $f(t_k;x_k)$ by $\Delta_k$, but the claimed suboptimality bound additionally requires the minimum value $f^*(t_k)$ to be nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $t_k>t_{k-1}$ for every $k\ge1$. Suppose that for each $k\ge1$ there are $j^*(k-1)$ and $L$ such that $f(t_k;x_k)\le f(t_{k-1};x_k)\le f^*(t_{k-1};x_{k-1,j^*(k-1)};L)$. Define $\Delta_k=f^*(t_{k-1};x_{k-1,j^*(k-1)};L)$ for $k\ge1$ and $\Delta_0=f(t_0;x_0)$. If $f^*(t_k)=\min_x f(t_k;x)$ and $f^*(t_k)\ge0$ for every $k\ge0$, then $f(t_k;x_k)-f^*(t_k)\le\Delta_k$ for every $k\ge0$. Without the nonnegativity condition, $f^*(t_k)\le f(t_k;x_k)$ alone does not imply the displayed upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The preceding selected residual bounds the next starting function value. It also bounds the next suboptimality gap when the corresponding minimum value is nonnegative; merely knowing that the minimum is no larger than the current value is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall k\ge0:\quad f(t_k;x_k)-f^*(t_k)\le\Delta_k;\qquad f^*(t_k)\le f(t_k;x_k)\text{ without }f^*(t_k)\ge0\text{ is insufficient}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Total internal-iteration bound for process (2.3.22)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The displayed expression must be finite; in addition to positive logarithm arguments, this excludes \(x=1/2\), where \(\ln(2(1-x))=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in(0,1)\), \(\epsilon>0\), and \(Q_f>0\). Initialize process (2.3.22) with \(t_0>t^*\) and \(x_0\), and suppose every displayed logarithm has positive argument and the displayed bound is finite. Then the total number of internal iterations is at most \[\left[\frac{1}{\ln(2(1-x))}\ln\frac{t_0-t^*}{(1-x)\epsilon}+2\right]\left[1+\sqrt{Q_f}\ln\frac{2(Q_f-1)}{x}\right]+\sqrt{Q_f}\ln\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\max_{1\le i\le m}\{f_0(x_0)-t_0;f_i(x_0)\}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated initialization and domain conditions, the total number of internal iterations of process (2.3.22) is bounded by the displayed product of an outer-stage logarithmic factor and an inner-work factor, plus a logarithmic initial-residual term. The formula is undefined at x equal to one half.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Comparison of strongly convex and smooth regularized values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares two quadratic regularizations using the strong-convexity and gradient-Lipschitz parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be differentiable, suppose that \nabla f is L\text{-Lipschitz}, and suppose that f is \mu\text{-strongly convex}, where 0<\mu\le L. For \alpha>0, define f^*(t;\bar x;\alpha):=\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{f(x)+\frac{1}{2\alpha}\|x-\bar x\|^2-t\right\}, let x^*(t;\bar x;\alpha) denote its unique minimizer, and define g_f(t;\bar x;\alpha):=\alpha^{-1}(\bar x-x^*(t;\bar x;\alpha)). Then, for every t\in\mathbb{R} and \bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n, f^*(t;\bar x;\mu)\ge f^*(t;\bar x;L)-\frac{L-\mu}{2\mu L}\|g_f(t;\bar x;L)\|^2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every level and center, the quadratic-regularized value with parameter mu is at least the value with parameter L minus (L−mu)/(2 mu L) times the squared norm of the L-regularized gradient mapping, provided the objective is differentiable, L-smooth, and mu-strongly convex with 0 < mu <= L.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*(t;\bar x;\mu)\ge f^*(t;\bar x;L)-\frac{L-\mu}{2\mu L}\|g_f(t;\bar x;L)\|^2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth Approximation of an Affine Euclidean Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the Euclidean operator norm \(\|A\|_{2,2}\); the zero-operator case is included and yields smoothness parameter zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be \(q(x)=\|Ax+b\|_2\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Estimating Sequence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an estimating sequence for an arbitrary real-valued function on \(\mathbb R^n\).

Sequences \(\{\phi_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}\), with \(\phi_k:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), and \(\{\lambda_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}\subset[0,\infty)\) form an estimating sequence for \(f\) if \(\lambda_k\to0\) and, for every \(k\ge0\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\phi_k(x)\le(1-\lambda_k)f(x)+\lambda_k\phi_0(x).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratically regularized linearized finite-max subproblem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean auxiliary model formed from component linearizations of a finite maximum over a prescribed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, let \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable at \(x_0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and let \(\gamma>0\). Define the auxiliary problem
\[
\min_{x\in Q}\left\{\max_{1\le i\le m}\bigl[f_i(x_0)+\langle\nabla f_i(x_0),x-x_0\rangle\bigr]+\frac{\gamma}{2}\lVert x-x_0\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, its epigraph formulation is
\[
\min_{x\in Q,\,t\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{t+\frac{\gamma}{2}\lVert x-x_0\rVert^2\right\}
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
f_i(x_0)+\langle\nabla f_i(x_0),x-x_0\rangle\le t,
\quad i=1,\ldots,m.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearize each component at x₀, take the finite pointwise maximum, and add a positive Euclidean quadratic term. Introducing an epigraph variable produces the equivalent constrained formulation with one affine inequality per component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in Q}\left\{\max_{1\le i\le m}\bigl[f_i(x_0)+\langle\nabla f_i(x_0),x-x_0\rangle\bigr]+\frac{\gamma}{2}\lVert x-x_0\rVert^2\right\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\min_{\substack{x\in Q,\,t\in\mathbb{R}\\f_i(x_0)+\langle\nabla f_i(x_0),x-x_0\rangle\le t\;\forall i}}\left\{t+\frac{\gamma}{2}\lVert x-x_0\rVert^2\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Well-defined constrained gradient mapping and model sandwich bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States both uniqueness for the displayed quadratic max model and the conditional pointwise and optimal-value sandwich bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix t\in\mathbb{R}, \bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n, and \gamma>0, and define f_\gamma(t;\bar x;x):=\max\left\{f_0(\bar x)+\langle\nabla f_0(\bar x),x-\bar x\rangle-t+\frac{\gamma}{2}\|x-\bar x\|^2,\ f_i(\bar x)+\langle\nabla f_i(\bar x),x-\bar x\rangle+\frac{\gamma}{2}\|x-\bar x\|^2\ (i=1,\ldots,m)\right\}. The components of this max model belong to \mathcal{S}^{1,1}_{\gamma,\gamma}(\mathbb{R}^n), and the constrained gradient mapping x_f(t;\bar x;\gamma) is therefore well defined and unique. Moreover, if f(t;\cdot)\in\mathcal{S}^{1,1}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^n) with 0<\mu\le L, then, for every x\in\mathbb{R}^n, f_\mu(t;\bar x;x)\le f(t;x)\le f_L(t;\bar x;x), and f^*(t;\bar x;\mu)\le f^*(t)\le f^*(t;\bar x;L).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the same positive quadratic term to the affine objective and constraint models produces a max model with a unique associated constrained gradient mapping. If the original max-type function has curvature parameters mu and L with 0 < mu <= L, its values lie pointwise between the mu- and L-models, and the corresponding minimum values obey the same ordering.
assumptions_latex: f_\gamma(t;\bar x;x)=\max\left\{f_0(\bar x)+\langle\nabla f_0(\bar x),x-\bar x\rangle-t+\frac{\gamma}{2}\|x-\bar x\|^2,\ f_i(\bar x)+\langle\nabla f_i(\bar x),x-\bar x\rangle+\frac{\gamma}{2}\|x-\bar x\|^2\ (i=1,\ldots,m)\right\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_f(t;\bar x;\gamma)\text{ is well defined and unique};\qquad f_\mu(t;\bar x;x)\le f(t;x)\le f_L(t;\bar x;x)\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n;\qquad f^*(t;\bar x;\mu)\le f^*(t)\le f^*(t;\bar x;L)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric residual bound for the two-level scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional outer-iteration decay estimate; positivity of the parameter increments is required for the displayed normalized residuals to be real and defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $0\le\kappa<\tfrac12$, let $t_{k+1}=t^*(x_{k,j(k)},t_k)$, and suppose $t_{k+1}>t_k$ for all $k\ge0$. Assume that, for every $k\ge1$, $2(1-\kappa)\,\frac{f^*(t_k;x_{k,j(k)};L)}{\sqrt{t_{k+1}-t_k}}\le\frac{f^*(t_{k-1};x_{k-1,j(k-1)};L)}{\sqrt{t_k-t_{k-1}}}$. Also assume $t_1-t_0\ge f^*(t_0;x_{0,j(0)};\mu)$, $f^*(t_0)\le t^*-t_0$, $f^*(t_0;x_{0,j(0)};L)\le\frac{1}{1-\kappa}f^*(t_0;x_{0,j(0)};\mu)$, and $t_{k+1}-t_k\le t^*-t_0$ for all $k\ge0$. If $f^*(t_k;x_{k+1};L)=f^*(t_k;x_{k,j^*(k)};L)\le f^*(t_k;x_{k,j(k)};L)$, then $f^*(t_k;x_{k+1};L)\le\frac{t^*-t_0}{1-\kappa}\left[\frac{1}{2(1-\kappa)}\right]^k$ for every $k\ge0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the parameter increments are positive, the normalized terminal residual contracts as stated, the initial and increment bounds hold, and the selected internal iterate has no larger residual than the terminal iterate, the selected residual decreases geometrically with ratio one divided by twice one minus kappa.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The quantities L, μ, x_f(y;L), and g_f(y;L) are the max-type first-order update and associated gradient mapping defined by the surrounding problem model.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric outer-gap iteration bound and contraction boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extracted proposition assumes $\kappa\in(0,1)$, but its logarithmic iteration guarantee is valid as written only in the contraction regime $0<\kappa<\tfrac12$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $t^*>t_0$ and suppose $0<t^*-t_{n+1}\le[2(1-\kappa)]^{-1}(t^*-t_n)$ for every $n\ge0$. If $0<\kappa<\tfrac12$ and $\epsilon>0$, define $N(\epsilon)=\frac{1}{\ln(2(1-\kappa))}\ln\frac{t^*-t_0}{(1-\kappa)\epsilon}$. Then every integer $n\ge0$ satisfying $n\ge N(\epsilon)$ obeys $t^*-t_n\le(1-\kappa)\epsilon$, so at most $\max\{0,\lceil N(\epsilon)\rceil\}$ full iterations are required. The extracted range $\kappa\in(0,1)$ is insufficient: the formula is undefined at $\kappa=\tfrac12$, and the recurrence factor is at least one for $\kappa\ge\tfrac12$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The outer target gap yields the stated logarithmic iteration guarantee when kappa is below one half. At one half the formula is singular, and above one half the displayed recurrence is not a contraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\quad n\ge\frac{\ln\left(\frac{t^*-t_0}{(1-\kappa)\epsilon}\right)}{\ln(2(1-\kappa))}\Rightarrow t^*-t_n\le(1-\kappa)\epsilon;\quad \kappa\ge\tfrac12\text{ does not support this guarantee as written}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Well-definedness of the max-type quadratic gradient mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers a finite maximum of differentiable components linearized at one point and minimized over an arbitrary nonempty closed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty and closed, let \gamma>0, and let f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x), where every f_i is differentiable at \bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n. Define f_\gamma(\bar x;x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\{f_i(\bar x)+\langle\nabla f_i(\bar x),x-\bar x\rangle+\frac{\gamma}{2}\|x-\bar x\|^2\} for x\in Q. Then f_\gamma(\bar x;\cdot) has strongly convex max-type components with parameter \gamma, the problem \min_{x\in Q}f_\gamma(\bar x;x) has a unique solution, and X_f(\bar x;\gamma)=\arg\min_{x\in Q}f_\gamma(\bar x;x) is a singleton. Hence the induced point-valued gradient mapping x_f(\bar x;\gamma) is well defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite maximum of functions differentiable at the base point, adding the same positive quadratic term to every affine component makes the max-type model strongly convex. On any nonempty closed feasible set, that model has exactly one minimizer, so the induced gradient mapping is single valued.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly Convex Estimating-Sequence Recurrence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs an estimating sequence from global quadratic lower models of a smooth strongly convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathcal S_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^n)\) with \(0<\mu\le L\), let \(\phi_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be convex, let \(y_k\in\mathbb R^n\) be arbitrary, and let \(\alpha_k\in(0,1)\) satisfy \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty\). Set \(\lambda_0=1\) and recursively define \[\lambda_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)\lambda_k,\] \[\phi_{k+1}(x)=(1-\alpha_k)\phi_k(x)+\alpha_k\left[f(y_k)+\langle\nabla f(y_k),x-y_k\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-y_k\|^2\right].\] Then, for every \(k\ge0\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\phi_k(x)\le(1-\lambda_k)f(x)+\lambda_k\phi_0(x),\] and \(\lambda_k\to0\). Hence \(\{(\phi_k,\lambda_k)\}\) is an estimating sequence for \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth strongly convex function, repeatedly averaging the current auxiliary function with a quadratic first-order lower model at any chosen point produces an estimating sequence, provided the averaging weights lie strictly between zero and one and have divergent sum. The associated product weights tend to zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential objective-gap decay from internal contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional linear convergence of the internal process. Finiteness of the minimum is needed to define the gaps, and the final bound by the initial function value additionally requires $f^*(t_k)\ge0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix $t_k$ and suppose $f^*(t_k):=\inf_x f(t_k;x)\in\mathbb R$. Let $x_{k,0}=x_k$ with $f(t_k;x_k)<\infty$. If $q_f\in(0,1]$ and $f(t_k;x_{k,j+1})-f^*(t_k)\le(1-\sqrt{q_f})(f(t_k;x_{k,j})-f^*(t_k))$ for every $j\ge0$, then, with $\sigma=\sqrt{q_f}$, $f(t_k;x_{k,j})-f^*(t_k)\le2(1-\sqrt{q_f})^j(f(t_k;x_k)-f^*(t_k))\le2e^{-\sigma j}(f(t_k;x_k)-f^*(t_k))$ for all $j\ge0$. If moreover $f^*(t_k)\ge0$, then this quantity is at most $2e^{-\sigma j}f(t_k;x_k)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform one-step contraction of a finite internal objective gap gives geometric and exponential decay with exponent square root of q_f. The final comparison with the initial function value is valid only when the minimum value is nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective Error Bound from an Estimating Majorant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers an upper bound by the minimum of an auxiliary convex combination into an objective-value convergence bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) attains its minimum at \(x^*\), and write \(f^*=f(x^*)\). Let \(\phi_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), let \(\lambda_k\in[0,1]\) with \(\lambda_k\to0\), and define \(\phi_k(x)=(1-\lambda_k)f(x)+\lambda_k\phi_0(x)\) and \(\phi_k^*=\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\phi_k(x)\). If \(f(x_k)\le\phi_k^*\) for every \(k\), then \[0\le f(x_k)-f^*\le\lambda_k\bigl(\phi_0(x^*)-f^*\bigr)\quad\forall k,\] and consequently \(f(x_k)-f^*\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the target function attains its minimum and every iterate value is bounded above by the minimum of the corresponding convex combination of the target and initial auxiliary functions, then its objective error is at most lambda_k times the initial auxiliary gap at an optimizer. Thus the objective values converge to the optimum when lambda_k tends to zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Root localization and lower bound for regularized model values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves the stated comparison, monotonicity, root-selection condition, and strict parameter ranges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n and \bar t<t^*. Suppose that, for some \kappa\in(0,1), f^*(\bar t;\bar x;\mu)\ge(1-\kappa)f^*(\bar t;\bar x;L). Assume that s\mapsto f^*(s;\bar x;\mu) is decreasing and that t^*(\bar x,\bar t) is defined so that f^*(\bar t;\bar x;\mu)>0 implies t^*(\bar x,\bar t)>\bar t. Then \bar t<t^*(\bar x,\bar t)\le t^*. Moreover, for every t<\bar t and every x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad f^*(t;x;L)\ge2(1-\kappa)f^*(\bar t;\bar x;L)\sqrt{\frac{\bar t-t}{t^*(\bar x,\bar t)-t}}.

In addition, every earlier level t and every center x satisfy the stated square-root lower bound for the L-regularized value.

knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Smooth Objective Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic minimization with globally Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable. The unconstrained \(L\)-smooth objective model is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d} f(x),\qquad \|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\quad	ext{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d,\]
where \(L>0\). A solution is any \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}f(x)\), when this set is nonempty. Without convexity, the basic first-order target is instead an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point satisfying \(\|
abla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a differentiable function over Euclidean space using a globally Lipschitz gradient; solutions are global minimizers, while nonconvex analysis commonly targets small gradient norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}f(x)\) is the unconstrained smooth model, with \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\).

notation.meaning: global Lipschitz constant of the gradient

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unconstrained Smooth Minimization Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of the finite-dimensional problem, its optimal points, and the attained optimal value when a minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(f\in\mathcal F_L^{1,1}(\mathbb R^n)\), the unconstrained smooth minimization problem is
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x).
\]
Any \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)\) is an optimal point. When such a point exists, its attained value is denoted by \(f^*=f(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unconstrained smooth minimization problem minimizes a function in the class F_L^{1,1} over all of R^n. Every global minimizer is an optimal point, and when a minimizer exists its attained objective value is denoted by f*.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)\Longrightarrow x^*\text{ is optimal and }f^*=f(x^*)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order local oracle and joint accuracy criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Source-specific oracle-access and approximate-solution definitions for unconstrained smooth strongly convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(n\ge1\), \(\mu>0\), and \(L\ge\mu\). Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)\) with \(f\in\mathcal S^{\infty,1}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^n)\), and let \(x^*\) be its unique minimizer with \(f^*=f(x^*)\). A first-order local black-box oracle returns \((f(x),\nabla f(x))\) when queried at \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). For \(\epsilon>0\), a point \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) is an approximate solution with accuracy \(\epsilon\) if \[f(\bar x)-f^*\le\epsilon\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\bar x-x^*\|^2\le\epsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For this unconstrained smooth strongly convex problem class, a local first-order oracle returns the objective value and gradient at each query. The source's ε-accuracy criterion requires both objective error at most ε and squared distance to the unique minimizer at most ε.
assumptions_latex: x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)\text{ is the unique minimizer}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal O_f(x)=(f(x),\nabla f(x));\qquad \bar x\text{ is an approximate solution with accuracy }\epsilon\iff f(\bar x)-f^*\le\epsilon\ \text{and}\ \|\bar x-x^*\|^2\le\epsilon.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A joint problem, oracle, and approximate-stationarity specification for unconstrained smooth minimization; convexity is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The class $\mathcal G_*$ consists of problems $\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)$ with $f\in C^{1,1}_L(\mathbb R^n)$ and a value $f^*\in\mathbb R$ satisfying $f(x)\ge f^*$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unconstrained Smooth Convex Minimization Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the unconstrained problem for an L-smooth convex objective, including the strongly convex regime when \(\mu>0\), together with optimal solutions and the optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(\mu\ge 0\), \(L>0\), and \(f\in\mathcal S^{1,1}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^n)\). The associated unconstrained problem is \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x).\] A point \(x^*\in\mathbb R^n\) is an optimal solution if \(f(x^*)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). When such a point exists, the optimal value is \(f^*:=f(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an L-smooth convex objective on Euclidean space, possibly strongly convex, the unconstrained problem minimizes the objective over the whole space. An optimal solution has value no greater than that at any other point, and this value is denoted by f*.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is optimal}\iff (\forall x\in\mathbb R^n)\ f(x^*)\le f(x),\qquad f^*:=f(x^*)\text{ when an optimizer exists}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unconstrained smooth convex optimality and minimizing sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the smooth convex problem model and minimizing-sequence terminology with the convex first-order optimality characterization; the latter is cross-indexed to convex analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and twice continuously differentiable on its open domain, and suppose its infimum is attained. Write \(p^\star=\inf_x f(x)\). For every \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \nabla f(\bar x)=0.\] A sequence \(\{x^{(k)}\}_{k\ge0}\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) is a minimizing sequence if \(f(x^{(k)})\to p^\star\). For a prescribed tolerance \(\epsilon>0\), the stated termination test is \(f(x^{(k)})-p^\star\le\epsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an attained unconstrained problem with a twice continuously differentiable convex objective on an open domain, a domain point is optimal exactly when its gradient vanishes. A sequence is minimizing when its objective values converge to the optimal value. The stated stopping test requires an objective gap no greater than epsilon.
assumptions_latex: f:\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is convex and twice continuously differentiable on its open domain}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall \bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f:\ \bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\iff\nabla f(\bar x)=0;\quad f(x^{(k)})\to p^\star\text{ defines a minimizing sequence};\quad f(x^{(k)})-p^\star\le\epsilon\text{ is the stated termination test}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General set-constrained minimization model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the basic finite-dimensional optimization model and its principal variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the problem is \(\min\{f(x):x\in\Omega\}\). The set \(\Omega\) is the feasible or constraint set, and any \(x^\star\in\Omega\) attaining the smallest objective value is a minimizer; minimizers need not be unique. Maximizing \(f\) over \(\Omega\) is equivalent to minimizing \(-f\) over \(\Omega\). The problem is unconstrained when \(\Omega=\mathbb R^n\). A membership condition \(x\in\Omega\) is a set constraint; a representation \(\Omega=\{x:h(x)=0,\ g(x)\le 0\}\) gives functional constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a real-valued objective over a feasible set. Any feasible point attaining the smallest objective value is a minimizer, and several minimizers may exist. Maximization is equivalent to minimizing the negative objective. The model is unconstrained when the feasible set is the whole space; equality and inequality descriptions of the feasible set are functional constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(d\in\mathbb{N}\) and a differentiable objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), the exact local first-order oracle is the mapping
\[\mathcal{O}_f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^d,\qquad \mathcal{O}_f(x)=\bigl(f(x),\nabla f(x)\bigr).\]
Given an initial query \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), a deterministic first-order method may, for each \(k\in\mathbb{N}_0\), generate
\[x_{k+1}=\Phi_k\bigl((x_0,\mathcal{O}_f(x_0)),\ldots,(x_k,\mathcal{O}_f(x_k))\bigr),\]
where \(\Phi_k:(\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^d)^{k+1}\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is a fixed update map. This oracle supplies the objective value and gradient at each queried point, but no Hessian or higher-order derivative information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact local first-order oracle returns the objective value and gradient at a queried point. A deterministic first-order method chooses each subsequent query through a fixed map of the accumulated query-and-response history.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Source-Defined Differentiability via a Radial Little-o Remainder
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract's Euclidean differentiability definition uses a single scalar remainder function of the radius; this is stronger than the usual direction-dependent Fréchet little-o formulation and is preserved literally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable at \( ar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) in the stated sense if there exist \(
abla f( ar x)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(o:[0,\infty)	o\mathbb{R}\) such that \(o(0)=0\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{r\downarrow0} rac{o(r)}{r}=0\), and, for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(f(y)=f( ar x)+\langle
abla f( ar x),y- ar xangle+o(\|y- ar x\|)\). The affine map \(y\mapsto f( ar x)+\langle
abla f( ar x),y- ar xangle\) is called the linear approximation at \( ar x\), and \(
abla f( ar x)\) is called the gradient there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the extract, differentiability at a point means that the function equals its affine first-order approximation plus one scalar remainder depending only on the distance from that point, with the remainder negligible relative to that distance. knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Objective Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric positive-semidefinite quadratics used to expose first-order spectral dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex quadratic objective model on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) has the form
\[f(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Qx-b^{\mathsf T}x+c,\qquad Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succeq0,\]
with gradient \(\nabla f(x)=Qx-b\). It is \(L\)-smooth when \(\lambda_{\max}(Q)\le L\), and it is \(\mu\)-strongly convex when \(Q\succeq\mu I\) for some \(\mu>0\). A minimizer exists exactly when \(b\in\operatorname{range}(Q)\), in which case every minimizer solves \(Qx^\star=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex quadratic is determined by a symmetric positive-semidefinite Hessian. Its extreme eigenvalues control smoothness and strong convexity, and minimizers solve the associated linear system.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)=Qx-b\), with smoothness and curvature determined by the spectrum of \(Q\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gram Operator of a Linear Matrix Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic representation of the squared Frobenius norm of a matrix-valued linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given $A_1,\ldots,A_p\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and
\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p x_iA_i,
\]
define $G:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^p$ by
\[
\langle Gx,x\rangle=\langle A(x),A(x)\rangle_F\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^p).
\]
Equivalently, its matrix entries are
\[
G^{(i,j)}=\langle A_i,A_j\rangle_F,
\qquad i,j=1,\ldots,p.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gram operator associated with the matrices A_i represents the squared Frobenius norm of their linear combination. Its i,j entry is the Frobenius inner product of A_i and A_j.

children.title: Quadratic Momentum Stability

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Momentum Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schur-stability condition for constant-parameter heavy-ball dynamics on positive-definite quadratics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the heavy-ball iteration
\[x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha(Qx_k-b)+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1})\]
on a quadratic with \(Q\succ0\), the error in an eigendirection of eigenvalue \(\lambda\) obeys
\[z_{k+1}=(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)z_k-\beta z_{k-1}.\]
This mode is asymptotically stable exactly when both roots of
\[r^2-(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)r+\beta=0\]
lie in the open unit disk. For real parameters, the equivalent inequalities are \(|\beta|<1\), \(\alpha\lambda>0\), and \(\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta)\). Stability on the entire spectrum requires these inequalities for every \(\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heavy-ball stability reduces to a second-order scalar recurrence in each eigendirection. All characteristic roots must lie strictly inside the unit disk for every eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Quadratic momentum is stable exactly when \(|\beta|<1\), \(0<\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta)\) for every \(\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(Q)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Descent Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic upper model for an L-smooth function on a convex subset of a Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a convex subset of a Euclidean space \(\mathbb E\), and let \(f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be \(L\)-smooth on \(D\), where \(L\geq0\). Then, for all \(x,y\in D\), \[f(y)\leq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|x-y\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An L-smooth function on a convex set lies below its first-order approximation plus one half L times the squared distance between the two points.

source_refs.locator: 10.3 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Nonconvex Case p. 272

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(d\in\mathbb{N}\), a differentiable function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), a base point \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and a trial curvature \(M>0\), define
\[Q_M(y;x)=f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{M}{2}\|y-x\|^2.\]
A trial point \(y\in\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfies the local quadratic upper-model condition when
\[f(y)\le Q_M(y;x).\]
If \(\nabla f\) is \(L_{x,y}\)-Lipschitz on a neighborhood of the segment joining \(x\) and \(y\), then the condition holds whenever \(M\ge L_{x,y}\). In gradient backtracking, one may test \(y_M=x-M^{-1}\nabla f(x)\) and increase \(M\) until the displayed condition holds. If \(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz on a fixed neighborhood of \(x\), then this procedure accepts for all sufficiently large \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local quadratic upper-model test compares the objective at a proposed point with a quadratic model based at the current point. A Lipschitz constant valid near the tested segment guarantees the test when the trial curvature is at least that constant; local Lipschitz continuity near the base point therefore ensures eventual acceptance by gradient backtracking.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Nonconvex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth minimization without convexity, measured by first-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The smooth nonconvex regime consists of objectives \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) that are differentiable, bounded below, and have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, without requiring convexity. A point \(x\) is first-order stationary when
\[\nabla f(x)=0,\]
and is \(\varepsilon\)-stationary when
\[\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon.\]
Because stationarity need not imply global or local optimality, the canonical global performance criterion for a first-order algorithm is reduction of \(\min_{0\le k<K}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\), rather than a guaranteed global objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without convexity, smooth first-order analysis targets points with small gradient. Such stationarity does not by itself certify local or global optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime uses \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon\) as its standard approximate-solution criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex smooth minimization measured by global objective suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The smooth convex regime consists of differentiable functions \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\]
and
\[\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d.\]
When \(X^\star=\operatorname*{argmin}f\) is nonempty, the canonical accuracy criterion is the global gap \(f(x)-f^\star\le\varepsilon\), where \(f^\star=\min f\). Every stationary point is then a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity turns first-order stationarity into global optimality. Algorithmic accuracy is naturally measured by objective value above the global minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(X^\star\ne\varnothing\) when an objective-gap criterion is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)=0\) implies \(x\in X^\star\), and accuracy may be measured by \(f(x)-f^\star\le\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smoothable Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines smoothability through a family of convex differentiable underapproximations with uniform additive error and inverse-parameter gradient smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex function \(h:\mathbb E\to\mathbb R\) is \((\alpha,\beta)\)-smoothable, where \(\alpha,\beta>0\), if for every \(\mu>0\) there exists a convex differentiable \(h_\mu:\mathbb E\to\mathbb R\) such that, for every \(x\in\mathbb E\), \[h_\mu(x)\le h(x)\le h_\mu(x)+\beta\mu,\] and \(\nabla h_\mu\) is Lipschitz with constant \(\alpha/\mu\). Such \(h_\mu\) is called a \(1/\mu\)-smooth approximation of \(h\) with parameters \((\alpha,\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function is (alpha,beta)-smoothable when, for every positive smoothing parameter mu, it has a convex differentiable underapproximation whose uniform error is at most beta times mu and whose gradient is alpha/mu-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\mu>0\;\exists h_\mu\text{ convex and differentiable}:\quad h_\mu\le h\le h_\mu+\beta\mu,\quad \operatorname{Lip}(\nabla h_\mu)\le \alpha/\mu.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Calculus of Smooth Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers a fixed positive smoothing parameter and preserves both uniform approximation error and inverse-parameter gradient smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\mu>0\). (a) If, for \(i=1,2\), \(h^i:\mathbb E\to\mathbb R\) is convex and \(h_\mu^i\) is a \(1/\mu\)-smooth approximation of \(h^i\) with parameters \((\alpha_i,\beta_i)\), then for all \(\gamma_1,\gamma_2\ge0\), \[\gamma_1h_\mu^1+\gamma_2h_\mu^2\] is a \(1/\mu\)-smooth approximation of \(\gamma_1h^1+\gamma_2h^2\) with parameters \((\gamma_1\alpha_1+\gamma_2\alpha_2,\gamma_1\beta_1+\gamma_2\beta_2)\). knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Strongly Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth strongly convex minimization with finite condition number and unique minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The \((\mu,L)\)-smooth strongly convex regime consists of differentiable functions \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) such that, for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\),
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|y-x\|^2\]
and
\[\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|,\]
where \(0<\mu\le L\). Such an objective has at most one minimizer; when a minimizer \(x^\star\) exists, it is unique. The ratio \(\kappa=L/\mu\) is the condition number governing standard first-order contraction factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity adds uniform positive curvature to smooth convexity, yielding a unique minimizer when attained and a finite condition number controlling first-order convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is simultaneously \(\mu\)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth, with condition number \(\kappa=L/\mu\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyak-Lojasiewicz Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Polyak–Łojasiewicz gradient dominance for a differentiable objective with an attained minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, let \(f^*=\min_x f(x)\), and assume the minimum is attained. The function satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition with constant \(\mu>0\) when
\[
\frac{1}{2}\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2^2\geq \mu\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Consequently, every stationary point is globally minimizing, although the condition alone does not require \(f\) to be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PL geometry bounds objective suboptimality by the squared gradient norm, so every stationary point is a global minimizer without requiring convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac12\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2^2\geq\mu(f(x)-f^*)\) for all \(x\), hence \(\nabla f(x)=0\Rightarrow f(x)=f^*\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the global differentiable PL inequality and its stationary-point consequence are standard and mathematically unambiguous

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Growth Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global quadratic growth measured by Euclidean distance to the minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have finite attained minimum \(f^*\), and write \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin} f\neq\varnothing\). The function has quadratic growth with modulus \(\mu>0\) on a set \(D\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) when
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq \frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^2\qquad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
Taking \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\) gives global quadratic growth; choosing a neighborhood of \(X^*\) gives the local form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic growth lower-bounds objective error by a positive multiple of squared distance to the solution set.

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance from x to the minimizer set.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Error-Bound Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient-residual error bound for unconstrained differentiable minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}f\). A gradient-residual error bound holds on \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with constant \(\kappa>0\) when
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq \kappa\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2\qquad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
The condition is global when \(D=\mathbb{R}^n\), and local when \(D\) is a specified neighborhood or objective sublevel set containing \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gradient-residual error bound controls distance to the minimizer set by the gradient norm on a specified region.

knowledge_statements.title: Growth–Error-Bound Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential equivalence for convex differentiable objectives; constants need not be sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and continuously differentiable, with nonempty closed minimizer set \(X^*\) and finite value \(f^*\). Suppose \(\nabla f\) is globally Lipschitz. Then the following global properties are equivalent: there exists \(\mu>0\) such that
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^2,
\]
and there exists \(\kappa>0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq\kappa\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2.
\]
Both inequalities are required for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\); the analogous equivalence holds on compatible invariant sublevel regions under corresponding local hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex smooth objectives, global quadratic growth is equivalent to a global gradient-residual error bound, up to changes in constants.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\mu>0\) satisfying quadratic growth if and only if \(\exists\kappa>0\) satisfying the gradient-residual error bound.
review_flags: exact equivalence hypotheses and localization regime require authoritative source confirmation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The global equivalence is plausible under the stated convex smooth hypotheses, but its exact assumptions and constants require authoritative confirmation. The additional local-equivalence sentence does not specify the compatible regions, invariance requirement, or corresponding local hypotheses precisely enough to review independently.

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Gradient Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Riesz-gradient and steepest quadratic-model representation in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For differentiable \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), the Euclidean gradient \(g=\nabla f(x)\) is the unique vector satisfying \(Df(x)[d]=\langle g,d\rangle_2\) for every direction \(d\). For any \(\alpha>0\), the Euclidean gradient step is equivalently characterized by
\[
d_x=\operatorname*{argmin}_{d\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\langle g,d\rangle_2+\frac{1}{2\alpha}\lVert d\rVert_2^2\right\}=-\alpha g.
\]
Thus the gradient identifies the locally steepest direction under the Euclidean quadratic penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Euclidean gradient represents the derivative, and its negative scaled value uniquely minimizes the regularized local linear model.

notation.meaning: Directional action of the derivative at x on d.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Euclidean Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed symmetric positive-definite metric and its preconditioned gradient representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive definite. Define \(\langle u,v\rangle_M=u^{\mathsf T}Mv\), \(\lVert u\rVert_M=(u^{\mathsf T}Mu)^{1/2}\), and the dual norm \(\lVert g\rVert_{M^{-1}}=(g^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}g)^{1/2}\). For differentiable \(f\), its metric gradient is \(\operatorname{grad}_M f(x)=M^{-1}\nabla f(x)\), and
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{d}\left\{\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle_2+\frac{1}{2\alpha}\lVert d\rVert_M^2\right\}=-\alpha M^{-1}\nabla f(x).
\]
Hence a fixed metric acts as a fixed preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite metric replaces the Euclidean gradient by the preconditioned vector obtained by applying the inverse metric matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}_M f(x)=M^{-1}\nabla f(x)\) and the metric step equals \(-\alpha M^{-1}\nabla f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Gradient relative to the M-inner product.

knowledge_statements.title: General-Norm Steepest Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Steepest regularized direction under an arbitrary finite-dimensional norm and its dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) be a norm on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), with dual norm \(\lVert g\rVert_*\). Given \(g=\nabla f(x)\) and \(\alpha>0\), choose
\[
d_x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{d\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\langle g,d\rangle+\frac{1}{2\alpha}\lVert d\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
Every such direction satisfies \(\lVert d_x\rVert=\alpha\lVert g\rVert_*\), \(\langle g,d_x\rangle=-\alpha\lVert g\rVert_*^2\), and the minimum model value is \(-\alpha\lVert g\rVert_*^2/2\). The direction may be nonunique when the squared norm is not strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General-norm steepest descent minimizes a linearized objective plus squared norm penalty, with direction magnitude governed by the dual gradient norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_x\) minimizes the regularized linear model and satisfies \(\lVert d_x\rVert=\alpha\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_*\).

notation.meaning: Dual norm of the chosen primal norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean steepest direction and sufficiently small descent steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean steepest-direction characterization and the local decrease consequence of a negative directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable at \(x_k\), and write \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). If \(g_k\neq0\), then
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|p\|_2=1}p^Tg_k=\left\{-\frac{g_k}{\|g_k\|_2}\right\}.
\]
Moreover, for any \(p_k\) satisfying \(g_k^Tp_k<0\), there exists \(\bar\epsilon>0\) such that
\[
f(x_k+\epsilon p_k)<f(x_k)\qquad\text{for every }0<\epsilon<\bar\epsilon.
\]
The Euclidean steepest-descent method uses the direction \(p_k=-g_k\), with its scaling determined by the chosen step length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point with nonzero gradient, the unique Euclidean unit direction of greatest instantaneous decrease is the normalized negative gradient. Any direction having a strictly negative inner product with the gradient decreases the objective for every sufficiently small positive step. Euclidean steepest descent uses the unnormalized negative gradient, with the step length supplying the scale.
assumptions_latex: g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\ne0\quad\text{for the normalized steepest-direction characterization}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a differentiable objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), an initial point \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), positive stepsizes \((\alpha_k)_{k\geq0}\), and a stopping tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\). At iteration \(k\), evaluate \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). If \(\lVert g_k\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon\), output \(x_k\); otherwise set
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k
\]
and continue. If no finite stopping time occurs, the output is the generated sequence \((x_k)_{k\geq0}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient descent repeatedly subtracts a positive stepsize times the exact Euclidean gradient and stops when the gradient norm meets tolerance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Best-iterate gradient bound for fixed-step gradient descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite-horizon gradient-norm guarantee for Euclidean gradient descent with stepsize $1/L$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f\in\mathcal{F}_{1,L}^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, let $x^*\in\arg\min f$, and set $R_0=\|x_0-x^*\|$. If $(x_k)_{k\ge0}$ is generated by the gradient method with constant stepsize $1/L$, then for every integer $T\ge3$ there exists $i\in\{0,\ldots,T\}$ such that $\|\nabla f(x_i)\|^2\le\frac{16L^2R_0^2}{(T+4)(T+6)}$. Equivalently, $\min_{0\le i\le T}\|\nabla f(x_i)\|\le\frac{4LR_0}{\sqrt{(T+4)(T+6)}}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For gradient descent with constant stepsize 1/L on the stated function class, every integer horizon of at least three contains an iterate satisfying the displayed gradient-norm bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective-Gap Bound for Fixed-Step Gradient Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-iterate bound for smooth convex gradient descent with a fixed step strictly between zero and \(2/L\); the zero-distance initialization is stated separately because the displayed source fraction becomes \(0/0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\mathcal F_L^{1,1}(\mathbb R^n)\) attain its minimum at \(x^*\), and set \(f^*=f(x^*)\). Let \(0<h<2/L\) and
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-h\nabla f(x_k),\qquad k\ge0.
\]
If \(x_0\ne x^*\), then for every \(k\ge0\),
\[
f(x_k)-f^*\le
\frac{2\bigl(f(x_0)-f^*\bigr)\|x_0-x^*\|^2}
{2\|x_0-x^*\|^2+h(2-Lh)k\bigl(f(x_0)-f^*\bigr)}.
\]
If \(x_0=x^*\), then \(x_k=x^*\) and \(f(x_k)-f^*=0\) for every \(k\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex differentiable function with L-Lipschitz gradient and an attained minimum, fixed-step gradient descent with 0<h<2/L obeys the stated rational objective-gap bound. Initialization at the chosen minimizer yields a stationary sequence with zero gap.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient descent can converge to a non-minimizing stationary point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nonconvex counterexample. The invariant-line conclusion holds for arbitrary real steps, but convergence does not; a particular valid step choice establishes the claimed possibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
f(x^{(1)},x^{(2)})=\frac12(x^{(1)})^2+\frac14(x^{(2)})^4-\frac12(x^{(2)})^2.
\]
Its stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(0,\pm1)$. The points $(0,\pm1)$ are isolated local minima, whereas $(0,0)$ is not a local minimum. For iterations
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-h_k\nabla f(x_k),\qquad h_k\in\mathbb R,
\]
initialized at $x_0=(1,0)$, one has $x_k^{(2)}=0$ for every $k$. In particular, choosing $h_k=1$ gives $x_1=(0,0)$ and $x_k=(0,0)$ for all $k\ge1$, so gradient descent can converge to a non-minimizing stationary point. Invariance alone does not imply convergence for arbitrary real steps; for example, $h_k=0$ leaves $x_k=(1,0)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated smooth quartic, (0,±1) are isolated local minima and (0,0) is stationary but not locally minimizing. Every gradient trajectory from (1,0) remains on the line with second coordinate zero. Unit steps reach (0,0), proving that gradient descent can converge to a non-minimizer. Arbitrary real steps do not all converge; zero steps provide an immediate failure case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k^{(2)}=0\ \forall k;\qquad h_k=1\ \forall k\implies x_k=(0,0)\ \forall k\ge1,\quad (0,0)\text{ is not a local minimizer}

Input differentiable \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), a fixed matrix \(M=M^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), positive stepsizes \((\alpha_k)\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\). \]
and update \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_k d_k\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step squared energy-norm contraction for exact-line-search steepest descent on a strongly convex quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx-b^Tx\) with \(Q=Q^T\succ0\), and apply steepest descent with exact line searches. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Condition-number consequences of the steepest-descent contraction factor
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-gap linear convergence, the isotropic one-step case, and deterioration of the worst-case bound with conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under exact-line-search steepest descent for \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx-b^Tx\) with \(Q=Q^T\succ0\), let \(\kappa(Q)=\lambda_n/\lambda_1\) and \(q=(\lambda_n-\lambda_1)/(\lambda_n+\lambda_1)=(\kappa(Q)-1)/(\kappa(Q)+1)\). Then \[f(x_{k+1})-f(x^*)\leq q^2\bigl(f(x_k)-f(x^*)\bigr),\] so the objective gaps converge at least linearly according to this worst-case bound. If all eigenvalues are equal, then \(q=0\) and the method reaches \(x^*\) in one step. As \(\kappa(Q)\) increases, \(q\) increases toward \(1\), so the bound deteriorates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quadratic bound gives linear convergence of objective gaps. Equal eigenvalues yield convergence in one step, while increasing the condition number drives the worst-case contraction factor toward one.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic rate of exact-line-search steepest descent near a nondegenerate minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eventual objective-gap contraction determined by the spectrum of the limiting Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable and the iterates generated by steepest descent with exact line searches converge to \(x^*\), where \(\nabla^2f(x^*)\succ0\). Let \(0<\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n\) be the eigenvalues of \(\nabla^2f(x^*)\). For every \[r\in\left(\frac{\lambda_n-\lambda_1}{\lambda_n+\lambda_1},1\right),\] there exists \(K\) such that, for every \(k\geq K\), \[f(x_{k+1})-f(x^*)\leq r^2\bigl(f(x_k)-f(x^*)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If exact-line-search steepest-descent iterates converge to a point with positive-definite Hessian, their objective gaps eventually contract by any squared factor strictly above the limiting spectral factor and below one.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean Steepest-Descent Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines steepest descent in the Euclidean metric, including its optional exact line search and search-direction decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} have continuous first partial derivatives and set g(x)=\nabla f(x)^T. Steepest descent generates x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g(x_k), where \alpha_k\ge 0. An exact line-search choice satisfies \alpha_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\ge 0}f(x_k-\alpha g(x_k)). Equivalently, the iteration is the composition of G(x)=(x,-g(x)) with a line-search map S.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable function, Euclidean steepest descent moves from each iterate in the negative-gradient direction using a nonnegative step. The step may be chosen by exact minimization along that ray, and the method decomposes into direction generation followed by line search.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g(x_k),\qquad \alpha_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\ge0}f(x_k-\alpha g(x_k))\ \text{when exact line search is used}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Accelerated steepest-descent recurrence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the acceleration parameters, gradient step, extrapolated iterate, and elementary parameter properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\beta>0\), set \(\lambda_0=0\) and, for \(k\ge0\), \[\lambda_{k+1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4\lambda_k^2}}{2},\qquad \alpha_k=\frac{1-\lambda_k}{\lambda_{k+1}},\] \[\widetilde x_{k+1}=x_k-\frac1\beta\nabla f(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)\widetilde x_{k+1}+\alpha_k\widetilde x_k.\] The parameters satisfy \(\lambda_k^2=\lambda_{k+1}(\lambda_{k+1}-1)\) for \(k\ge0\), and \(\lambda_k>k/2\) and \(\alpha_k\le0\) for \(k\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from lambda zero equal to zero, recursively compute the acceleration parameter, take a gradient step of length 1/beta, and combine the new and preceding gradient-step points. The lambda recurrence obeys its stated quadratic identity; from iteration one onward lambda exceeds k/2 and the extrapolation coefficient is nonpositive.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is differentiable at every evaluated iterate}
\widetilde x_k\text{ is initialized wherever the recurrence requires it}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Steepest descent with exact line search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean steepest descent using a gradient-norm stopping test and exact minimization along each negative-gradient ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ and $\varepsilon>0$, set $k=0$. At iteration $k$, compute $g_k=\nabla f(x_k)$. If $\|g_k\|\le\varepsilon$, stop. Otherwise set $d_k=-g_k$, choose $\alpha_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\ge0}f(x_k+\alpha d_k)$, set $x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k$, increment $k$, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from any point and a positive tolerance, stop when the gradient norm is at most the tolerance. Otherwise use the negative gradient as the direction, exactly minimize the objective over the nonnegative ray in that direction, update the iterate, and repeat.
